title: Karma
speaker: Karen DeCotis
summary: The talk explores how our intentions and actions shape our experiences, suggesting that karma is not just about punishment or reward, but also about understanding the interconnectedness of all things. While intention matters, the consequences of our actions can be unpredictable and influenced by factors beyond our control. By cultivating good character and taking action in the present moment, we can approach our lives with greater awareness and intention, rather than relying solely on external forces to shape our behavior.
topics: Buddhist concept of karma patterns of moral causality

sentences.text: Good morning.
Good morning, and thank you very much for coming to our Zen Alive Sunday program.
The Dharma talk today will be given by Karen DeCotis.
She is coming to us from Bozeman, Montana.
Thank you very much, Karen, for joining us.
And we appreciate that you are coming this great distance through Zoom.
Karen received transmission in 2019 and is, like I said before, the teacher for the Bozeman, Montana Zen group.
Thank you very much.
Good morning, everyone.
Thank you for being here.
Excuse my slow moving around.
Some of it is crowdedness, some of it is age.
But here I am, and thank you for the lovely service and the doanryo in one person, Kate, Kokiyo, Doan, Fukudo, and it was lovely to chant together.
I don't know you, but I recognize some names.
John Wiley, I saw Bob Andrews, Patricia Star.
Somehow I know your names, but I don't know why.
But thank you all for welcoming me.
Let's see, I'll tell you just a little bit about how we're doing in Montana.
Any of you who have looked at the news see Montana as this bright red spot, hotspot of COVID right now.
Just when we thought, like everyone did earlier in the summer, that, oh, it's time to find a place to meet again, the Delta variant hit.
And so we're mostly on Zoom, although we now meet Monday nights in person, the Zen group does.
Mixed.
We also have Zoom on Monday nights.
We meet also Sunday mornings on Zoom, and we're studying Joko Beck's book, Every Day Zen, and slowly, slowly getting through it.
And we sit every morning, Monday through Friday at six.
How many of you are in Bellingham actually?
Like wave, and some of you are not.
Okay.
Well, good to see you, Bellingham.
I would love to visit sometime.
And Kate, are you in a Zendo of some sort?
**Participant:** No, this is actually my ground floor.
And I just converted it.
Well, brought my equipment down here.
**Karen DeCotis:** Yeah.
Yeah, it's lovely to see.
Okay.
So what else to warm us up?
Everybody doing okay, mostly?
Healthy?
Showing up?
Good.
Great.
Okay.
Well, I apologize in advance, I'm using you as guinea pigs.
This is my second attempt: I'm going to attempt a talk on karma.
Some of you who have practiced for a while know that in Zen, we might loosely throw the word around, but that we don't really study karma, or talk about it the way we do everything else.
But I found some info, I found a chapter on it, and I'll tell you about that.
I want to speak about it because it all started with "I should read that book by Norman," The World Could Be Otherwise.
Some of you, I'm sure you know it.
It's on the six paramitas, and he brings forth the notion of imagination.
So I started reading it.
And I got through generosity.
And then I got to morality.
And then somewhere along the line, oh, the last full moon, we were going to all meet together and do a full moon ceremony.
And then the weather turned in Bozeman, as it often does abruptly.
We were having this beautiful fall, and then we got dumped eight inches of snow like last Monday.
Well, something similar happened the full moon night, so we didn't get to meet in person at our friend's house.
We met at the church where we're meeting now, and we did a sort of recite the Bodhisattva ceremony.
And it got me thinking again about morality and the precepts.
I was reading Norman's book and then I remembered I had Dale Wright's book.
He has a chapter on morality that is just amazing, and the whole part on karma got me going.
Sometimes when I think about morality and the precepts, I think about what we teach kids in school: just behave and be kind.
Right?
It really boils down to just behave and be kind.
So what Dale Wright emphasizes in his book on the six perfections is the cultivation of character.
And, again, I've been working in the school system a little bit.
In one of the rooms, a teacher has posted: character is doing the right thing even when no one is looking.
So this idea of building a good character, of being upright and knowing in each moment what may be the appropriate responses.
I'm getting a little bit in a bind because I never really write my talks out.
Sometimes when I'm in a new situation I do, but I'm not good at reading my written talks.
So hang in there with me, I'll click in here in a minute.
Morality, the ethical conduct, has often been quoted or referred to as the way to start the path.

Until we are following certain basic guidelines in how we are in relationship to each other, not killing, not stealing, not misusing sexuality, and how we are with ourselves, not speaking in harsh terms about other people, not disparaging the Dharma, not intoxicating self, until we are doing these practices we really can't find benefit in sitting still or following a path.
So much so that even ethical conduct has been equated with meditation, in that it is a practice one does every day.

And in fact, sometimes the paramitas are pared down to just ethical conduct, meditation and wisdom, those three, even though when you study down a paramita, generosity, they'll say, well, that's the most important one.
If you are practicing generosity, then you are really on the path.
So like Suzuki Roshi, whatever we're talking about is the most important thing.
In this chapter on morality, he talks a lot about the precepts and how following the precepts is a really great guideline for living a daily life, and karma is part of the functioning of our conduct.
Again, we don't speak of it so much technically or spiritually in Zen.
A lot of times we do it informally, sometimes we joke about it.
Which refers to its more historical and conventional or linear aspects, in that from the Hindu tradition, the sense of karma was very personal.
If you were born into a certain cast, it was because of karma from a past life, and your job was to live in that cast, do the best you could and hope for a better rebirth.
So it was very much about rebirth or reincarnation, and it was very linear.
It was: do this and this will happen, live a good life and your next life will be better.
So what is our experience with karma?
Do we see it as immediate and clear, sensible outcomes, effects from our thoughts and actions?
A good place to start is: what do we think karma is, why do we talk about it, and why is it related to morality and ethical conduct?
The translation of karma from the Sanskrit is action, as many of you know.
When we think about action, we think about not only our action physically or socially but our words and our thoughts.
So karma is what we're doing with ourselves.
The Shambhala dictionary calls it the action that produces a fruit, and when it is ripe, it falls on the one responsible.
So if I have a certain thought or say a certain thing, it produces an effect, and when that ripens, it falls back on me.
That is the sort of historical definition.

It's related in that way to the eighth consciousness that some of you may have studied, the Alaya Vijnana, where the seeds are reposited for us to either bring forth or practice with keeping quiet the seeds that we don't want to come to fruition.
What we're talking about with karma is in the moral domain, so we're talking really just about ethical conduct.
There are many things we do that we could consider neutral, except for how we bring ourselves to it.
There's a way to wash the dishes that is just washing the dishes, and then there's a way to wash the dishes that could be conditioned by a bunch of whatever we're bringing to it.
So karma, whether it's good or bad, is conditioned by our volition, by our intention.

When things are done outside of our volition, or maybe even unconsciously, that's a little bit more of a gray area about whether we're personally responsible for that karma, although we should pay attention.

I know by definition things that are unconscious are unconscious, yet still in our reciting of our vows, we promise to bring that forward, to open up to everything that may be operating within us, all of our conditioning.

So when we think of the fourth skandha, that volitional activity, the grooves in our psyche that operate us, that we want to become more conscious of so we can be making choices that are wholesome and beneficial, that is a place to practice.
We have our body, speech, and mind, and we have that fourth skandha, which is where so many things get grooved in, get habituated, and a lot of our karma is related to that.
One of the things to remember that helps us, I think a lot, is that the intention around the action determines the effect of karma more than the action itself.

I'm going to say that again because something that I'm studying recently, and that maybe some of you are, flies in the face of that: the intention of the action determines the karmic effect more than the action itself.
Any of you studying any kind of racial justice or equity know the distinction between intention and impact.
Yes, some of you are familiar with that distinction.
I think that is also an important distinction to remember, that the road to hell is paved with good intentions.
So intention is very important and it matters.
However, impact and what we actually do also matters.
I think in this model, though, the effect of karma is related more to our intention rather than what we actually do and whatever mistakes we actually make.
But I don't know if I'm right about that.
Like I said, this is a pilot talk.
It's pilot talk number two.
Okay.
I want to read some of this.
It will probably be very clarifying.
From Dale, he writes:
*The six perfections: skill in moral life entails cultivating an understanding of the Buddhist concept of karma, patterns of moral causality that are thought to govern all human transformation.
Although karma literally means action, the principle of karma concerns the connection between the quality of an act and the nature of the consequences that follow from it.
Actions of a particular quality give rise to consequences of a corresponding kind.
And this is thought to be a law inherent in the nature of things.
Much of the Indian vocabulary of karma evolved out of agricultural metaphors.
Karma is conceived as a seed that ripens into a specific fruit.*
But the interpretations of all of this are quite diverse within Buddhism, just to know.
And it says:
*Not all acts are thought to be productive of karma, because karma is restricted to those done with volition, intention or purpose.*
Like I said, on Sunday mornings our group is studying Joko Beck's Everyday Zen, which I highly recommend.
It's so practical and she's like a big dose of cold water in the face.
Really getting you to find out what you're up to.
And the chapter we've been stuck on for a couple weeks is called "It's Okay."
So the teaching is, can you be okay with not only your circumstances, but your response to your circumstances?
If my circumstances are, I have not enough money, and I'm very uptight about it, or I'm very repressed about it or I'm very panicked about it.
And hold on.
You know how thoughts come and then they just go away.
It was all there, and now only half is there.
Oh, our Zen group is part of the Bozeman Dharma Center, and we gave up our space last fall.

Our good friend Michelle, who's a Zen student and is sewing her priest robes, is the Dharma Center coordinator, so she's putting things on social media and doing the website and the newsletter, and she wanted to use that quote from Joko Beck about things being okay, even when they're not okay.
At first she had a picture of a black man in some kind of agony.
And then she had a girl, a white girl, with a similar sort of picture.
And she was very nervous about posting either one of these, because for the black man she didn't want people to think, oh, you've been oppressed for hundreds of years but just get over it.
She didn't want it to be misinterpreted.
You really have to practice with "it's okay" in a very clear Zen context, and you can't just say, oh, it's okay.
And then for the white girl, she was afraid that it was like, oh, there it is again, a white girl not getting her way and reacting, and it's okay.

So everything is open to interpretation, and she decided to go the safe route and not even use the quote at all, because out of context, it may seem like we should just be okay with things the way they are.
I'll get to that again in a minute.
So, like everything we study in Zen, who we're being is the most important thing.
The connection between the quality of how we are acting is so much more important than what we actually do.
In other words, sometimes we have to say no about something.
We have to do a generous no, a no that makes the person you're saying no to feel seen and loved.
It seems that all acts generate consequences that shape the character of who we are, so our choices matter.
So actions reap rewards and punishment in proportion to their moral quality.
The effects happen now in this life, in the next life.
But the effects take place internally, without the intervention of a kind of divinity.
I want to get to that in just a moment.
As we talk more about the choices we make, there are different dimensions of the Buddhist doctrine of karma.
I just want to go through this so we can sort of land where karma actually operates in our life and where it doesn't.
According to Dale Wright, there are four areas of karmic justice to consider.
The first one was very enlightening for me, and it's called cosmic justice.
We imagine that the world operates according to a kind of cosmic justice, that things are going to work out, that people who do bad things are going to have some bad effects.
And if we're really good, we'll have some good effects.
And that if as a nation we are a good and kind and just nation, we will prosper, things like that.
But we have the experience that this is not always so.
We expect good and evil consequences to match up to what happens, but they don't.
Many of you might remember a book that came out, I think it was in the 70s, *When Bad Things Happen to Good People*.
That just sums it up right there.
I know a woman, and I don't mean to load you up with a difficult thing, but I know a woman who two weeks ago lost her two children in a car accident.
We grew up hearing that karma has something to do with this, but that was a traffic accident.
It was not necessarily in the moral domain, but now she has this effect.
The old way of thinking about karma was, oh, well, she and her children are paying for something from a past life.
I don't think that's necessarily true.
It seems that the cosmic justice should be connected, but it isn't.
It turns out that the universe, without a divinity, without a sort of God, is fairly neutral and doesn't really care about justice in the way we think about it.
It's just operating according to, I don't know what to call it, like, physics.
It's just operating according to nature, it just moves along.
So sometimes really healthy people get cancer, and people who smoke and drink and don't exercise live to 90, like my mom.
Right.
So things are not on the cosmic level that clear.
It seems like something's going on that is impersonal and doesn't have anything to do with how you're being.
That doesn't mean don't be a certain way, it just means on the cosmic level.
We probably should, even though we feel like it should be that way.
That's our human idea, and there is a universe that's operating, including but beyond just the human sense of things.
The human sense, that's our experience, right, that a lot of things happen that seem like they shouldn't happen.
Kind of sucks.
Okay, social justice.
The realm that this is about is how we as Buddhists want to engage in the world.

We have to be careful that if we think the concept or the operation of karma is that things will take care of themselves, like if I'm good, good things will happen, or if I'm generous, I'll become wealthy, if we think—
We may use our Buddhist practice to become quite passive, thinking that we don't really have to do anything to help the world, because everybody's just living out their karma.
But that is not actually helpful.
And our vows as Bodhisattvas: we want to think that there are ways we can help beings without just relegating them to their karma, thinking, well, maybe in their next life things will be better.
We do not want to acquiesce in the face of oppression.
We do not want to let harm happen, even if we think, oh, the person receiving that harm must be paying for karma from a previous life.
I don't think this is a helpful way to think about karma.
I think we help in the moment.
Our commitment to nonviolence doesn't mean that we live a life of non-action.
If justice is not in the structure or the fabric of the cosmos, and it doesn't operate on its own in a social world, then humans should take it up and not leave it to chance.
We should participate in karma, in the fruits of action, through our own activity, our own following the precepts and committing to our Bodhisattva vow.
We think the nature of reward and punishment is expected to follow what Dale Wright calls our morally relevant actions.
So if you're really generous, you give a lot of money or time to a situation, you probably expect something.
At the very least you expect to feel good or feel like you're a good person.
You might expect people to notice, and you might not want to admit that to yourself.
That might be a little more subconscious.
Or you might expect that your activity will make things change and actually help people.
I give $5 a month to Greenpeace, and I don't think it's doing anything, but I do it.
But what do I expect from that?
One way to think about our expectations is the expectations of external effects, rewards.
They're what they call contingent, they're dependent, we can't control them.
So sometimes you could do something really wonderful and be appreciated for it.
And I think that appreciation could be a really positive thing in that it strokes the ego, but it also might encourage you to keep doing that.
So just because we get an external reward doesn't mean it's a bad thing, or an egocentric thing.
You can make use of it.
But if we do it to get that, we're missing the point of our activity.
In education, I'm working with after school directors who are trying to run after school programs.
These parents haven't had after school help for a year and a half, and now they have it.
They're sending their kids because they need to work or they need to get stuff done, and the kids are wearing masks, and the new program coordinators are untrained.
We have all this social emotional learning we're trying to give kids.
The going line is not "what's wrong with you?", which is what you want to say when a kid is really pissing you off.
The right question is no longer "what is wrong with you?"
The right question is "what happened to you?"
There's a reason you're behaving this way, you're expressing a need.
But in an after school program with 50 kids running around, you don't have time to sit and be everything for that kid.
And there's this one woman who believes that parents should still swat their kids.
Who am I to say, right?
I got swatted and whatever.
But the point is, I said to her, we've lost some of the old tools for dealing with kids to get perfect behavior, and we can't shame them.
So what do we do?
We have to actually be in relationship with them.
Some of these people are not on board with that at all.
They want perfect behavior, they expect a certain outcome, and they're trying to get something in the external.
We don't think about punishing kids anymore, but when kids are being a certain way, it's hard not to fall back into wanting to punish them.
But they don't get it.
A lot of times humans are like kids, we don't get it.
A punishment doesn't necessarily deter us from morally unwholesome activity.
For instance, anyone who has ever dealt with drinking or drugs could wake up feeling terrible, and you would think that punishment would be enough to divert them from doing that again.
And we all know, or overeating, or watching too much TV, or being too uptight and correct about the Dharma.
We can be all stuck on the Dharma.
But these are external things: we're looking to be seen a certain way and getting a certain goodie.
The internal effects are only available to us internally, and they're the ones that support our practice and actually transform the world, because they cultivate our character.
This is how I believe, and I think Dale Wright is saying, that the world transforms.
Like the Chinese said, when the individual is upright, the family is upright; when the family is upright, the community is upright, and so on and so on.
We can take care of our own behavior.
That may not be enough, but it is the place to start.
The internal effects of upright moral behavior shape our character.
From Dale Wright, we can summarize this by saying:
*How you comport yourself morally has at least three ramifications.
It shapes your character and helps determine who or what you become.
It helps shape others and the society in which you live now and into the future.
And it encourages others to treat you in ways that correspond to your character.
They will often do unto you as you have done unto them, although not always.*
So there's always that contingency that bad things happen to good people.
And one last thought:
*Thus, insofar as we can think this matter through, some dissociation between merit and external rewards is important to maintain.*
And that's part of our offering of merit, not holding on to it, but giving it away.
The last bit is just trying to bring the sense of emptiness or interdependence into the notion of karma.
We are not an individual self running on our own power with no other effects.
We're completely interdependent.
So is karma.
So if something happens to you, like these two little kids who died in a car accident, and their dad survived, and now he lives with that.
He lives with that.
That's enough of a karmic effect, although even if he ran the stop sign, it wasn't a moral transgression, but he still has something to live with.
And the karmic part of it will be, how does he bring himself to that practice?
But think of all the effects, all the elements that went into that happening.
The reason he was in Idaho with his children is because a divorce happened, and because the mom is from Idaho.
And think of the truck driver and what was going on for him, and think of the conditions of the road, and think of the time of day, and think of the people's internal state: what were they doing?
Were they distracted?
Were they laughing?
So many elements and factors go into any moment.
There's no way to pinpoint a certain thing and say, this is the cause.
And although we rely on causes and conditions to help mollify the things we go through, these causes and conditions are from way, way beyond us, from the past.

The past is so much pressing upon us, which is why zazen practice and getting to know yourself, and knowing something about your own psychological history, your family history, the way you're thrown to be, helps you sort out your overall karmic situation.
Someone once said to me, "Do you want to know your karma?
Look at your life."
When you think of that, it's a big practice.
There's so many things in my life that are wonderful, right?
I've lived a long time, I have health, I have income, I have friends, I have this practice, I have this opportunity, I have the best dog in the world.
I live in a beautiful place.
So many karmic effects that are wonderful, whether they're karmic or not, it could just be the neutral universe operating.
And then there are the things that don't work in my life.
But are they the direct result of what I did yesterday, or this accumulation of a whole lifetime?
We can't know the actual causes and conditions, we can just bow down to them and try to work within them with some grace.
I don't know if I've been near as clear as I've wanted to be, because I think I'm still working with the notion of karma as not being just a moral thing, but just in general.
But when you think about it, when we talk together, you guys can come up with examples too.
There are effects that happen that are cause and effect, like physics.
If I drop this book, it will fall to the ground.
I don't think there's a moral component to that, but there is an effect.

But not every effect may be a karmic effect, because, as Dale Wright says, in several respects, rebirth, and the reason he brings up rebirth is us thinking, okay, maybe in my next life things will be better, or for those other people.
Maybe in nine generations, Blacks will have a better life, like that.
*Rebirth stands in the way of an effort to understand karma in purely ethical terms.

Rebirth encourages us, one, to assume a concept of cosmic justice for which we have insufficient evidence; to ignore issues of justice in this life on the grounds that justice will be done in future lives;* like that's just being passive and not engaging; *to focus our hopes on external rewards for our actions, like wealth and status in a future life, rather than on the construction of character in this life; and to conceive of our lives in strictly individual terms as a personal continuum through many lives.*

In other words, Karen's had several million lives up till now and I'll have future lives, and what I do matters to my rebirth, *rather than collectively where individuals share in a communal destiny, contributing their own lives and efforts towards enlightenment for all.*
So I think, at the very least, what it's done for me is it's helped bring karma into the moral realm, but it's made it much more fuzzy for me.
What affects what?
Because the interdependence of things is something we can love, we can bow down to that, we can praise emptiness, we can know we are living in emptiness, but can we understand it?
Can we pull it apart?
Can we really connect up the dots to why things happen the way they do?
So again, here we are in Zen, living with knowing less than when we started.
I hope this has been incredibly useful to you.
I'm interested in what you might think about karma, or cause and effect, or morality.
Since there's 12 of us, you can just go like this and unmute and talk.
Is that the way you guys do it?
Is that good?
Okay.
All right.
**Participant:** Hi there.
Hi, I'm Desiree.
**Karen DeCotis:** Hi Desiree.
**Participant:** What comes to mind when we talk about karma for me is my root teacher Thich Nhat Hanh's reminder that it is not just individual, but it is.
